body.text: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the only Brazilian politician to win the presidency after trailing in the first round, was at the lowest point in his political life eight years ago. On the eve of a 580-day imprisonment on convictions the Supreme Court would later annul, finding that the trial judge had been partial, Lula told the crowd gathered around him: “I am an idea. And there is no point in trying to destroy ideas.”

Such defiance at the edge of the abyss has a number of precedents among leaders of the Latin American Left. When Fidel Castro reunited with his brother Raul and a few survivors of the Granma expedition in the foothills of the Sierra Maestra in December 1956, just days after the expedition had been nearly wiped out, he declared that they had “now won the war”. It would be years before they actually achieved the Cuban Revolution.

Lula’s weapon was never the gun but the ballot. He returned from prison to defeat the far-right Jair Bolsonaro (who had openly praised Brazil’s erstwhile military dictatorship) in 2022. On October 25, 2026, he held on to power by defeating Jair Bolsonaro’s son, Flávio Bolsonaro. Electoral victory is not new to the machinist-turned-unionist-turned-politician. He is set to begin a fourth term as the head of Latin America’s largest country. But what made this election remarkable was the manner of it and the circumstances around it, even if the term ahead may prove the most difficult yet for the octogenarian.

When Lula demitted office in 2011, after eight years in power, Latin America was firmly at the crest of the “pink tide”. Left and centre-left parties governed nation after nation in the continent, and Lula was the standard-bearer of its moderate and centre-left strain. Today, the region is gripped by what historian Vijay Prashad terms the “angry tide", in which several right-wing and far-right leaders, many openly endorsed by US President Donald Trump, have swept to power, from Argentina to Chile to Honduras.

The Right has appropriated the support of the poor and working-class voters, who turned to it to tackle crime and persistent inflation, and out of fatigue with left-wing governments that failed to deliver on their promises years after the exhaustion of the commodity booms that financed much of the Left’s welfare schemes. Only a handful of countries such as Mexico, led by Claudia Sheinbaum, and Uruguay, led by Yamandú Orsi, have held out alongside Lula’s Brazil.

Lula’s failure in the first round, when he finished with 45.2 per cent of the votes behind Flávio Bolsonaro’s 47 per cent, was despite the fact that his third term had delivered on the economic front. Growth rate was a cumulative 9.2 per cent between 2022 and 2025, much higher than the average for other South American countries. Unemployment fell from 9.3 per cent in 2022 to 5.4 per cent by mid-2026, and poverty dropped from 31.6 per cent to 23.1 per cent between 2022 and 2024. Inflation was also lower than in any presidential term since the hyperinflation-marred 1990s. According to Carbon Brief, annual deforestation in the Amazon more than halved from 11,594 sq km in 2022 to 5,731 sq km in 2025.

Lula’s trailing Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round had much to do with Brazilian families finding it increasingly difficult to service their household debt, largely due to the increase in the policy rate to 15 per cent in 2025 by the central bank. Brazilians did not significantly increase their borrowing during Lula’s third term (household debt stayed at about half the disposable income), but the share of income eaten up by repayments rose from 25.8 per cent in 2023 to 28.9 per cent by mid-2026.

The Center for Economic and Policy Research estimated that those earning up to twice the minimum wage were spending more than a third of their income on loan repayments, double the corresponding figure among the better-off. Defaults rose among poor borrowers, who increasingly relied on expensive personal loans and credit card debt. Critics on the left argue that the situation was not merely the outcome of the central bank’s actions, but of the Lula government’s own choices as well. Its debt renegotiation schemes eased only a part of the burden. While jobs were available, many of them were gig work and freelance contracts. None of the labour protections stripped away under Michel Temer, who took over as President in 2016 after Dilma Rousseff’s impeachment, were restored, leading to more precarity. This was reflected in the low support for Lula among the lower middle classes.
From sovereignty to welfare

Lula framed the battle against his rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, as one of retaining Brazil’s sovereignty. In 2025, that message served him well. When Trump imposed 50 per cent tariffs on Brazilian goods and sanctioned Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who was overseeing Jair Bolsonaro’s trial for plotting a coup after his 2022 defeat, Lula rallied the country under the banner of “Brasil Soberano” (Sovereign Brazil). The US later rolled back most of the tariffs. But by 2026, the pressure on Lula grew subtler and involved courts. A scandal around the collapsed Banco Master, the private bank whose founder had allegedly cultivated judges and their relatives, engulfed the Supreme Court. The Right capitalised on it to turn the first round into a contest over judicial corruption.

Lula’s campaign kept speaking about sovereignty and protecting Brazil’s rare earth deposits, which Flávio Bolsonaro had promised to open up to American companies. The electorate was not enthused; abstention in the first round reached 21 per cent, the highest since 1998. And the Right’s strength extended to the legislative Congress, with the Bolsonaros’ Liberal Party growing from 99 to 120 seats in the Chamber of Deputies and nearly doubling its previous tally in the Senate.

But once the first-round results were in, Lula engineered a remarkable turnaround. He conceded that he had presided over “the most disorganised campaign in history” and replaced its leadership. Instead of sovereignty and rare earths, Lula’s campaign now focussed on a shorter working week, an end to the six-day schedule, and relief for families reeling under heavy debt. He also campaigned on a 15 per cent increase in Bolsa Familia (Lula’s signature welfare scheme) payments that took effect in October. Lula admitted, for the first time in four years, that his government had made mistakes.

He was helped by the mobilisation of students, thousands of whom walked out of their campuses and marched through city centres in his support. The protests snowballed across the country, spontaneously and without party banners, held together less by devotion to Lula than by the need to defeat Bolsonarism. On the internet, Congressman André Janones set up a WhatsApp channel, “Lula’s Army”, that enrolled more than 10 million members within two weeks. Finally, abstention fell in the second round, and Lula won with 51.79 per cent of the votes to Flávio Bolsonaro’s 48.21 per cent. The first-round deficit of 2.2 million votes turned into a lead by about 4.4 million.

Meanwhile, two days after his defeat, Flávio Bolsonaro fled the country along with his wife and two daughters. Brazilian authorities investigating him for money laundering had cancelled his passports as part of a money-laundering investigation, but he crossed into Argentina by road and flew to Miami via Ecuador, with what Trump himself had offered as “a pass” into the country. From there, he farcically declared himself “the true president-elect of Brazil”, before deleting the claim and calling himself the country’s “leader” instead. The defeat of the Bolsonaros is a victory for institutionalism in Brazil, and a chance for the democratic centre-right, whose support base was usurped by a far-right that is anti-institutional, populist, and backed by the ultra-rich, to reclaim its ground.

Had Flávio Bolsonaro won, experts warned, he would have dramatically accelerated deforestation by increasing licences for agribusiness and mining, which would have affected the world’s lungs, the Amazon. Claudio Angelo of Brazil’s Climate Observatory called Lula’s re-election “the only thing standing between us and a wide destruction of the Amazon”. For the beleaguered Latin American Left as well, Lula’s victory is a major morale boost. Uruguay’s president Orsi was the first to call Lula to congratulate him.
Victory against the threat of Trump

A leftist’s victory in Brazil, Latin America’s largest and most populous country, is even more significant considering what has transpired during Trump’s second term. In December 2025, the administration’s National Security Strategy declared the Western Hemisphere its sphere of influence, reviving the Monroe Doctrine, originally meant to deter European interference in the Americas but used to justify US imperialist interventions for more than a century. Trump has used a policy of carrot and stick in Latin America, showering aid on right-wing allies such as Javier Milei of Argentina and Nayib Bukele in El Salvador while attacking Venezuela, sanctioning Colombia’s former President Gustavo Petro, bombing boats killing scores in the Caribbean Sea, and even meddling in elections in countries like Honduras.

On January 3, 2026, US forces attacked Caracas, abducted Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, and flew him to New York to place him on trial on unfounded charges. The US Energy Secretary soon declared that the US would control Venezuela’s oil sales indefinitely. Venezuela’s government does not even control the revenues from its own oil, which are managed by the US Treasury, while the interim President Delcy Rodriguez has signed deals which, according to Venezuelanalysis, hand over 17 prime oilfields to a private company backed by the Pentagon, in a shocking giving up of sovereignty. The Trump administration then cut off Cuba from oil supplies, asphyxiating the island nation subjected to a series of blackouts and food shortages.

In March 2026, Trump gathered a dozen allied Latin American leaders in Miami to launch the “Shield of the Americas”, a so-called coalition against drug cartels, during which he urged coalition partners to use their militaries. Flavio Bolsonaro advocated joining this grouping which is a thinly veiled opening for the US meddling in the internal affairs of these countries. Lula made sovereignty a central theme of his campaign, and while it was not the issue that won him the run-off, it remained the sharpest line between the two candidates.

Lula’s victory is also a boost to multilateralism. Brazil’s case for BRICS during Lula’s tenures has been about strategic autonomy, living “neither in China’s shadow nor in the shadow of the United States”, as Celso Amorim, Lula’s long-time Foreign Minister and his current Special Adviser, put it. Lula has pressed for trade within the bloc to be settled in local currencies rather than the dollar, and backed the New Development Bank, now headed by Rousseff, as an alternative to the Bretton Woods institutions. During its G20 presidency in 2024, Brazil commissioned a proposal for a global minimum tax on billionaires. Brazilian officials have been vocal about reforming the global financial architecture, which the West still dominates and which has long constrained development in the Global South. A Flávio Bolsonaro presidency, aligned with Trump, would have abandoned that project.
New challenges

Yet, the impressive victory does not take away from the new challenges that Lula would face in his fourth term. In the Chamber of Deputies, the Bolsonaros’ Liberal Party won 120 of the 513 seats. It holds 28 of 81 in the Senate in comparison to the Lula-led Partido dos Trabalhadores (Workers’ Party) or PT’s nine. Since Rousseff’s impeachment, legislators have sought to control the national budget, eroding presidential power. This was true of Lula’s third term as well. Lula had to back centrist candidates for presiding officers of both Houses, and his vetoes of a Bill loosening environmental licensing were overridden by the Congress. He also had to contend with a more independent central bank.

But negotiating and finding common ground has always been Lula’s strength. The historian John D. French, in his biography Lula and His Politics of Cunning (2020), showed how a machinist from the industrial belt around São Paulo led metalworkers’ strikes against the military dictatorship in the late 1970s, and helped build the PT from scratch. French describes Lula’s method as a willingness to talk to opponents without losing the ability to “stand up and fight, when needed”. He never abandoned his working class roots and reached out to the Brazilian poor instinctively.

In his third term, he kept the broad front he built before the 2022 election at arm’s length, sidelining centrist allies such as Simone Tebet and Vice President Geraldo Alckmin. He kept his inner circle to PT loyalists and trading ministries with transactional centrist parties for votes in the Congress. But with a stronger opposition today, he can no longer afford to do so. There is a useful precedent, however. In 2025, with the government campaigning hard to tax “billionaires, banks, and betting” and polls showing three in four Brazilians in its favour, the Chamber of Deputies unanimously passed an income tax reform that exempted those earning under R$5,000 a month and raised taxes on those earning over R$50,000.

Ultimately, Lula’s victory is indeed the victory of an idea in a country and a continent that has endured long spells of military dictatorship and served as a laboratory for neoliberal policies, punctuated in the recent decades by Left and centre-left governments that sought to upend the neoliberal consensus. Their record has been mixed at best. But the resilience of Lula and the PT is an exception of sorts. They returned to power and have held on to it in a hostile national and geopolitical environment. In doing so, they have kept alive the proposition that governments in deeply unequal Latin American economies can work for the benefit of the working classes.

To that extent, Lula’s claim on the eve of his imprisonment that he is an idea has been vindicated. What remains to be seen is whether the octogenarian, in what could be his final term, can convert a personal triumph into a durable movement. That movement would have to harness the agency of the millions of young people, the poor, and the workers who carried him through this election. Lula’s victory is a battle won for the Left, but converting Lulismo, his brand of welfare and redistribution, into an enduring project that outlives him is a war still being fought.
